{{Short description|American chemist (1920 – 2015)}}

'''George Warren Reed Jr.''' (1920–2015) was an [[African Americans|African American]] physicist known for his contributions to [[nuclear physics]] and his active involvement in civil rights activism.<ref name=":0" /> 

== Early life and education ==
George Warren Reed, Jr. was born in [[Washington, D.C.]] on September 25, 1920.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Munro |first=Robert |date=2011-08-24 |title=George Warren Reed Jr. (1920-2015) • |url=https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/reed-george-w-jr-1920/ |access-date=2024-03-19 |website=Black Past |language=en-US |archive-date=2023-10-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231007015046/https://www.blackpast.org/african-american-history/reed-george-w-jr-1920/ |url-status=live }}</ref> His mother graduated from [[Miner Teachers College]] and worked hard to provide for him.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |last=Crocker |first=Brittany |title=Bias kept black scientists out of Oak Ridge's atomic bomb work |url=https://www.knoxnews.com/story/news/2018/02/25/oak-ridge-manhattan-project-atomic-bomb-black-scientists/1083138001/ |access-date=2024-03-28 |website=Knoxville News Sentinel |language=en-US |archive-date=2024-01-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240117203159/https://www.knoxnews.com/story/news/2018/02/25/oak-ridge-manhattan-project-atomic-bomb-black-scientists/1083138001/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In early childhood, he was not allowed to work, even though the family had slight difficulties.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Overcoming racism and discrimination, Black Americans made significant contributions to the Manhattan Project |url=https://www.energy.gov/nnsa/articles/overcoming-racism-and-discrimination-black-americans-made-significant-contributions |access-date=2024-03-28 |website=Energy.gov |language=en |archive-date=2024-04-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240401071937/https://www.energy.gov/nnsa/articles/overcoming-racism-and-discrimination-black-americans-made-significant-contributions |url-status=live }}</ref> His only focus was to attend school and come home to complete all his assignments.<ref name=":1" /> Reed demonstrated exceptional academic aptitude and a strong interest in [[physics]] from an early age.<ref name=":2" /> 

Reed attended [[Howard University]], where he received a [[Bachelor of Science]] in chemistry in 1942 and a [[Master of Science]] in 1944.<ref name=":1" /> He then obtained his [[Doctor of Philosophy]] from the [[University of Chicago]] in 1952.<ref name=":0" />

== Career ==
Reed became a nuclear and [[Geochemistry|geo-chemist]] and worked on the [[Manhattan Project]] during [[World War II]], where he helped advance nuclear physics and [[Nuclear weapon|atomic weapons]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=George Warren Reed - Nuclear Museum |url=https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/profile/george-warren-reed/ |access-date=2024-03-28 |website=Atomic Heritage Foundation {{!}} National Museum of Nuclear Science and History |language=en-US |archive-date=2024-02-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240228001933/https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/profile/george-warren-reed/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Reed's main purpose was to make fissionable uranium to produce and sustain a nuclear reaction; he also examined the radiation of two chemicals, [[uranium]] and [[plutonium]], in different stages at the chemistry division of the [[Argonne National Laboratory]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> Reed’s work had a huge influence on the construction of the [[atomic bomb]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |title=LM Highlights 3 Accomplished Scientists in Honor of Black History Month |url=https://www.energy.gov/lm/articles/lm-highlights-3-accomplished-scientists-honor-black-history-month |access-date=2024-03-28 |website=Energy.gov |language=en |archive-date=2024-04-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240401021248/https://www.energy.gov/lm/articles/lm-highlights-3-accomplished-scientists-honor-black-history-month |url-status=live }}</ref> He studied, and research fission yields related to uranium and [[thorium]] to a definitive nuclear chain reaction.<ref name=":3" />

At the University of Chicago's [[Metallurgical Laboratory]], he worked alongside twelve famous Black Americans who made an impact to the projects mission.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /> He worked with individuals such as [[Ralph Gardner-Chavis]], Jasper Jeffries, [[Lawrence H. Knox|Lawrence]] and [[William Jacob Knox Jr.|William Jacob Knox]], [[Blanche J. Lawrence]], [[Carolyn Parker]], [[Ella Tyree]], and [[J. Ernest Wilkins Jr.|J. Ernest Wilkins]].<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> In light of Reed accomplishments, he was faced with racism with all his peers.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kates |first=Joan Giangrasse |date=2015-10-05 |title=George W. Reed, Argonne chemist who worked on Manhattan Project, dies at 94 |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/2015/10/05/george-w-reed-argonne-chemist-who-worked-on-manhattan-project-dies-at-94/ |access-date=2024-03-28 |website=Chicago Tribune |language=en-US |archive-date=2024-03-19 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240319213443/https://www.chicagotribune.com/2015/10/05/george-w-reed-argonne-chemist-who-worked-on-manhattan-project-dies-at-94/ |url-status=live }}</ref> At first, numerous black scientists who worked on [[Oak Ridge Seminary|Oak Ridge's]] atomic bomb were not recognized for their knowledge and expertise.<ref name=":1" /> In the 1940s due to [[Jim Crow laws|Jim Crow segregation]] laws only the white Americans and European refugee scientists could work freely on the site, black researchers could not.<ref name=":12">{{Cite web |last=Crocker |first=Brittany |title=Bias kept black scientists out of Oak Ridge's atomic bomb work |url=https://www.knoxnews.com/story/news/2018/02/25/oak-ridge-manhattan-project-atomic-bomb-black-scientists/1083138001/ |access-date=2024-03-28 |website=Knoxville News Sentinel |language=en-US |archive-date=2024-01-17 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240117203159/https://www.knoxnews.com/story/news/2018/02/25/oak-ridge-manhattan-project-atomic-bomb-black-scientists/1083138001/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Therefore a "Solid South" bloc of [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrats]] in Congress insisted that the new city reflected the Jim Crow segregation where African American could work.<ref name=":12" /> A "secret city" was built in the rural farmland of Anderson County, and African- American chemists and scientists were transferred to live there.<ref name=":12" /> Reed's contributions to the Manhattan Project in Oak Ridge by black scientists was not heard of.<ref name=":12" /> Reed and J. Ernest Wilkins worked with European refugee scientists [[Enrico Fermi]] and [[Leo Szilard]] in the Chicago Metallurgical Laboratory, known as the "Met Lab".<ref name=":2" /> Their research was moved to the south without receiving credit for their work.<ref name=":12" /> Since Reed and J. Ernest Wilkin's knowledge and expertise had a crucial role in the Manhattan Project in today's society they are now credited.<ref name=":2" /> Reed and his fellow peers were acknowledged the by [[National Nuclear Security Administration]] (NNSA) because it was the start of nuclear security missions, and it is a use in today's society.<ref name=":2" />

In 2006, Reed's son, Mark Morrison-Reed, interviewed Reed about his experiences with the Manhattan Project.<ref name=":4" /> Morrison-Reed donated the interview to the [[Atomic Heritage Foundation]].<ref name=":4" /> In the interview, Reed stated,<blockquote>My life story would be very different had not World War II intervened with the need to more fully utilize all the nation’s manpower and with the continued opening up of opportunities to all. [...] We didn’t know it at the time, but we were developing the atomic bomb. [...] I was trained as an organic chemist and we were purifying uranium, but at that time I was totally in the dark; we didn’t even talk to the people in the lab next to us.<ref name=":1" /></blockquote>After the war, Reed made significant contributions to the development of nuclear energy and its applications,<ref name=":0" /> including publishing over 120 scientific papers.<ref name=":3" /> From 1952 to 1968, Reed worked at the [[Argonne National Laboratory]] in the chemistry division as an associate chemist.<ref name=":3" /> He was then promoted to a senior scientist beginning in 1968. At the laboratory Reed did scientific research subsidiary of the university.<ref name=":2" />

Reed worked with the [[The Meteoritical Society|Meteoritical Society]] from 1970 to 1972 and [[NASA|National Aeronautics and Space Administration]] (NASA) from 1972 to 1980.<ref name=":3" /> While at NASA, he analyzed a sample of the [[moon rock]] from the [[Apollo 11|first moon landing]].<ref name=":4" /> His conclusion were the rock was contained with minerals not found on earth, a conclusion he made using a nuclear reactor.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":2" /> 

Along with his scientific endeavors, Reed was an active [[civil rights activist]], advocating for [[African Americans]]' equality and justice.<ref name=":4" />

== Personal life ==
Reed married Selina Edwards, with whom he had four children: Mark, Philip, Carole, and Lauren.<ref name=":1" />

Reed had been brought up in the [[Christian Science]] faith and was an attendee of the predominantly African American [[Eighth Church of Christ, Scientist]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=George Warren Reed's Interview (2006) - Nuclear Museum |url=https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/voices/oral-histories/george-warren-reeds-interview-2006/ |access-date=2025-03-03 |website=ahf.nuclearmuseum.org |language=en-US}}</ref>

Reed died in Chicago on August 31, 2015, from natural causes.<ref name=":3" />
